title: Scientists Decode Medieval Parchment DNA, Uncover Hidden Disease Secrets】
body:
Researchers have successfully extracted and sequenced ancient DNA from medieval parchment, uncovering a centuries‑old strain of sheeppox virus that plagued livestock across Europe and the Near East. The breakthrough, achieved by a multidisciplinary team of geneticists, historians, and conservation scientists, demonstrates that the very pages that recorded human history also preserved the genetic fingerprints of the animals that supplied the material. By comparing the viral genome recovered from a 13th‑century manuscript with modern isolates, the scientists traced the pathogen’s evolutionary trajectory and revealed how it spread long before contemporary farming practices amplified its impact.

The study focused on a collection of vellum codices housed in a European monastery, each made from the skin of sheep that were processed into parchment during the High Middle Ages. Using a minimally invasive sampling technique—tiny punches taken from the margins of the pages—the team isolated fragments of DNA embedded in the collagen matrix of the animal skin. While previous work had demonstrated the feasibility of retrieving host DNA from such sources, this is the first instance of reconstructing a complete viral genome from a non‑human artifact. Advanced metagenomic sequencing pipelines filtered out contaminant modern DNA, allowing the researchers to piece together a 150‑kilobase sheeppox virus genome with 98.7 % coverage.

Sheeppox, a contagious disease caused by a poxvirus of the genus Capripoxvirus, remains a serious threat to sheep and goats today, especially in regions where biosecurity measures are limited. Infected animals develop fever, skin lesions, and can suffer severe wool loss, weight reduction, and even death. Historical records from the medieval period describe “pustular eruptions” and “wasting of flocks,” but the precise causative agents were never confirmed. By aligning the ancient viral sequence with a global database of modern strains, the researchers identified a lineage that diverged from present‑day viruses roughly 1,200 years ago, predating the intensification of animal husbandry in the Middle Ages. This suggests that the disease was already endemic among pastoral communities and that its spread was facilitated by trade routes linking the Mediterranean, the Levant, and the Atlantic coast.

The implications of the discovery extend beyond veterinary epidemiology. The ability to retrieve pathogen DNA from parchment opens a new window into the history of zoonotic and livestock diseases, offering a complementary line of evidence to written chronicles and archaeological remains. “Every manuscript is a time capsule not only of human thought but also of the animals that contributed to its creation,” said Dr. Elena Marquez, the project’s lead geneticist. “By reading the molecular signatures preserved in these pages, we can reconstruct disease dynamics that shaped economies, diets, and even migration patterns.” Moreover, the methodology could be applied to other materials—such as leather, parchment‑bound maps, or even historical clothing—to track the spread of pathogens that left no written trace.

The findings also raise practical considerations for modern disease management. Understanding the deep evolutionary history of sheeppox can inform vaccine development by highlighting conserved viral regions that have persisted across centuries. In addition, the study underscores the importance of preserving historical artifacts in controlled environments; the integrity of ancient DNA is vulnerable to temperature, humidity, and handling, which could degrade valuable genetic information before it can be studied. Conservationists are now collaborating with geneticists to devise protocols that balance artifact preservation with scientific sampling.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to expand its survey to a broader corpus of medieval documents, including those from regions where sheeppox outbreaks were historically documented but remain genetically uncharacterized. By building a comprehensive map of ancient viral genomes, scientists hope to refine models of pathogen emergence and assess how past climate fluctuations, trade networks, and animal husbandry practices influenced disease evolution. As the boundaries between humanities and life sciences continue to blur, the parchment pages that once recorded human triumphs and tragedies may yet reveal the hidden biological narratives that shaped our shared past.
